land.text: Semigallia: the lower Mūša and Lielupe valleys, south-central Latvia and northern Lithuania, with Mežotne, Tērvete and Dobele

successors.note: The Livonian Order; in 1290 the Semigallians 'burned their last castle' at Sidrabė and moved south, so the land was largely emptied. The later Duchy of Courland and Semigallia (1561-1795) is a different state.

correction.text: Semigallia: the lower Mūša and Lielupe valleys, south-central Latvia and northern Lithuania, with Mežotne, Tērvete and Dobele

keyframe_review.note: New keyframe; Cliopatria has no row for Semigallia, and its Livonian Brothers of the Sword shapes draw the Order in Semigallia from 1210 although the pages keep it free until 1254-1290. The page places the Semigallians in 'the south central part of contemporary Latvia and northern Lithuania' on the lower Mūša and Lielupe, names the hillforts at Mežotne, Tērvete and Dobele, and the chieftaincies of Upmale, Dobele, Spārnene, Dobe, Rakte, Silene and Tērvete; no area. 1106 is the first dated mention. The Lithuanian half is a 40 km circle.

region.text: Semigallia: the lower Mūša and Lielupe valleys, south-central Latvia and northern Lithuania, with Mežotne, Tērvete and Dobele

ledger.note: 1106: the Semigallians defeat Polotsk. They 'defeated the invading army of Polotsk led by Prince Rogvolod Vseslavich in 1106', the earliest dated mention; the clans were united 'into a single state in the early 13th century' by Duke Viestards, a monarchy being 'an unconfirmed theory'.

region.text: Semigallia: the lower Mūša and Lielupe valleys, south-central Latvia and northern Lithuania, with Mežotne, Tērvete and Dobele

ledger.note: 1219: the crusaders invade Semigallia. 'The Semigallian-German alliance was canceled after a crusader invasion in Semigallia' (the Livonian Crusade page lists the Siege of Mežotne in 1219); Viestards then allied with the Lithuanians and Curonians. The page does not say the invaders held ground, so this is the first dated campaign, not a conquest.

region.text: Semigallia: the lower Mūša and Lielupe valleys, south-central Latvia and northern Lithuania, with Mežotne, Tērvete and Dobele

ledger.note: 1236: the Battle of Saule ends the Brothers' campaign. Semigallians 'attacked crusaders retreating to Riga after the Battle of Saule', the near-annihilation of the Livonian Brothers of the Sword; no land changes hands. The Livonian Crusade page adds that 'the surviving members of the Brothers of the Sword merged into the Teutonic Order of Prussia in 1237', so the contest counterpart passes to the Order.

region.text: Semigallia: the lower Mūša and Lielupe valleys, south-central Latvia and northern Lithuania, with Mežotne, Tērvete and Dobele

ledger.note: 1236: the contest continues against the successor Order (the Livonian branch of the Teutonic Order); the page dates no campaign that holds ground, so the land stays Semigallian, contested at confidence 1.

region.text: Semigallia: the lower Mūša and Lielupe valleys, south-central Latvia and northern Lithuania, with Mežotne, Tērvete and Dobele

ledger.note: 1254: the contest gives way to partial Order control (see the next entry).

region.text: Semigallia: the lower Mūša and Lielupe valleys, south-central Latvia and northern Lithuania, with Mežotne, Tērvete and Dobele

ledger.note: 1254: the Livonian Order partly subdues the Semigallians. 'The Livonian Order partly subdued the Semigallians in 1254'; the pages name no tribute, treaty or region, so the whole of Semigallia is drawn as under partial Order control (confidence 1) until the revolt of 1279.

region.text: Semigallia: the lower Mūša and Lielupe valleys, south-central Latvia and northern Lithuania, with Mežotne, Tērvete and Dobele

ledger.note: 1279: Duke Nameisis rises with Lithuanian support. After the Battle of Aizkraukle Traidenis 'supported a Semigallian revolt against the Livonian Order led by Duke Nameisis'.

region.text: Semigallia: the lower Mūša and Lielupe valleys, south-central Latvia and northern Lithuania, with Mežotne, Tērvete and Dobele

ledger.note: 1279-1290: the revolt under Nameisis reopens the contest; 'In the 1280s, the Livonian Order started a massive campaign against the Semigallians' (Livonian Crusade page); in 1287 'around 1400 Semigallians attacked a crusader stronghold in Ikšķile and plundered nearby lands', the main battle being near the Garoza river.

region.text: Semigallia: the lower Mūša and Lielupe valleys, south-central Latvia and northern Lithuania, with Mežotne, Tērvete and Dobele

ledger.note: 1290: the contest ends with the loss of the land (next entry).

region.text: Semigallia: the lower Mūša and Lielupe valleys, south-central Latvia and northern Lithuania, with Mežotne, Tērvete and Dobele

ledger.note: 1290: the Semigallians burn their last castle at Sidrabė and leave. 'The Semigallians resisted until 1290, when they burned their last castle at Sidrabene'; 'The Rhymed Chronicle's claim that 100,000 migrated to Lithuania' is cited.

region.text: Semigallia: the lower Mūša and Lielupe valleys, south-central Latvia and northern Lithuania, with Mežotne, Tērvete and Dobele

ledger.note: 1290: Semigallian independence ends with the burning of Sidrabė.

wars.name: Livonian Crusade

zones.text: Semigallia: the lower Mūša and Lielupe valleys, south-central Latvia and northern Lithuania, with Mežotne, Tērvete and Dobele

wars.outcome: The Semigallians attacked the crusaders retreating from Saule (1236), were partly subdued by the Livonian Order in 1254, revolted under Nameisis in 1279, attacked Ikšķile in 1287 and ended their resistance by burning their last castle at Sidrabė in 1290.
wars.note: Siege of Tērvete 1259, Battle of Tērvete 1270 (Traidenis and the Semigallians raid Livonia and Saaremaa), Battle of Karuse; the page gives the Siege of Mežotne as 1219.

certainty.note: Tribal lands without a boundary on the page; Semigallia is drawn as the Zemgale planning region plus a circle in northern Lithuania.

sources.title: Livonian Crusade
sources.note: 1205-1207 alliance, 1219 Mežotne, 1228, 1236 Saule, 1254, 1270 Tērvete, 1279 Nameisis, 1290 Sidrabė.

notes: Not a documented state until Viestards united the clans in the early 13th century (the page); no capital (Mežotne, Tērvete and Dobele are hillforts, not named capitals). Start 1106 is the first dated mention. 1254 'partly subdued' is carried as a vassal span with confidence 1 because no page names the land or the terms; the Order's gain of land is therefore not drawn. The Livonian Brothers of the Sword dossier flags that Cliopatria draws Semigallia as the Order's from 1210; the pages keep it free to 1254-1290. The dossier's wars entry is the Livonian Crusade as the Semigallians' page names it; the 1237 merger of the Brothers into the Teutonic Order moves the counterpart. The later Duchy of Courland and Semigallia is another state (duchy-of-courland, eu-14-h).
